transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's the driving. Specifically, the bridges. I work in HR over at the logistics company, and my commute, well, it shouldn't be that bad, but I find myself spending an hour every night just looking at maps, trying to figure out how to get to the office, or to a meeting, or even just to the grocery store, without having to cross any of those high overpasses or, God forbid, the suspension bridges. It's exhausting, honestly. And, you know, sometimes you just can't avoid it. Like last Tuesday, there was an accident on the lower route, and I had absolutely no choice but to take the high bridge. I tell you, my hands were clamped so tight on the steering wheel my knuckles were stark white. I didn't breathe the whole way across. I just stared straight ahead, rigid as a board, sweating through my shirt, just praying I'd make it to the other side without... well, I don't even know what I think is going to happen, but I just have to white-knuckle it the entire time. It's just getting to be too much, planning my whole life around avoiding these things.
Do you experience panic attacks when you are actually crossing the bridges?

Panic attacks? Well, I don't know if the doctors would call it a full-blown panic attack, you know, like you see on TV where a guy is hyperventilating into a brown paper bag or passing out, but I can tell you exactly what happens, and it's definitely not a calm drive in the park. It’s an immediate, physical thing. As soon as I even just see the bridge coming up in the distance—like, maybe I round a curve on the highway and there it is, looming up ahead with all those huge concrete pillars and steel cables—my chest just gets incredibly tight. It feels like someone wrapped a heavy leather belt around my ribs and just pulled it as tight as it goes. 

And my hands, they just start pouring sweat right there on the steering wheel. It gets so bad I actually worry my grip is going to slip on the leather, but I'm too scared to even take one hand off the wheel to wipe my palm on my slacks, so I just clamp down even harder. And my eyes... I can't look left, I can't look right, and I definitely can't look down at the water or the drop. I just start staring straight ahead. I lock my eyes on the license plate of whatever car happens to be in front of me, or just the white dashed lines on the pavement, and I get this intense tunnel vision. It's like my whole brain shuts down everything else and just focuses on the fact that I just have to make it to the other side. I'll turn off the radio, if someone is in the car with me I'll tell them they have to stop talking immediately, and I just sit there, chest tight, sweating, staring straight ahead until I finally feel solid, normal ground under the tires again. It feels like it takes hours to cross, even if it's only a minute. So I don't know if you'd call that a panic attack, but it sure feels like my body is going into some kind of overdrive every single time.
Is it just bridges that cause you this kind of anxiety, or are there other situations or places that trigger a similar reaction?

No, no, it's really just the bridges. I mean, I can fly on an airplane just fine, I don't mind tight spaces, elevators are no problem, spiders don't bother me... it's just those bridges. Especially the really high ones, you know, the ones over the bay. I mean, logically, I know they're perfectly safe. I watch the news, I know they do inspections, and thousands of folks drive over them every single day without a second thought. I see them zooming by, drinking their coffee, talking on their phones, totally oblivious. 

But for me... it's like my brain just completely ignores all that logic the second I get near one. I know those bridges over the bay are built fine, I really do, but when I get close to the approach, my mind just starts acting like... like the car could just go right over the side. Like a gust of wind is going to come out of nowhere and just blow my sedan right over the railing and into the water. Or like the steering wheel is suddenly going to jerk out of my hands and I'll just plunge over the edge. It makes absolutely no sense, I know it doesn't, but that's exactly what my brain tells me is going to happen. It's just this overwhelming feeling that the car is going to go over, and I can't shake it no matter how much I tell myself it's crazy. So, yeah, it's just the bridges. Nothing else gets to me like that. Just those big, high bridges.
Do you avoid bridges because of the fear of having this anxiety reaction, or because you're afraid of something bad happening while you're on the bridge?

Well, doctor, it's... I guess you could say it's a little bit of both, but mostly... mostly it's the feeling that something terrible is going to happen. Like I said, I get this image in my head that the car is just going to veer off, or the wind is going to catch it. And I know, I know it sounds ridiculous, and I tell myself it's ridiculous, but the fear is just so real in that moment. It's not just that I'm afraid of getting sweaty palms or a tight chest, although, believe me, that's incredibly unpleasant. Nobody wants to feel like they're having a heart attack on their way to a budget meeting. 

But it's the sheer terror of going over the edge that really drives it. I mean, I'll sit there with my maps for an hour, tracing these convoluted routes through residential neighborhoods and back roads, adding twenty, thirty minutes to my commute, just so I don't have to face that possibility. And then, if I do end up on one, the anxiety is so bad because I'm convinced I'm not going to make it across. So I'm avoiding the bridges because I'm terrified of falling, and the anxiety is just... it's just the physical reaction to that terror. Does that make sense? It's like, I don't want to feel the panic, sure, but the panic only happens because I'm so sure the car is going into the water.
Is your fear specifically of bridges, or is it more about the height of the bridges that bothers you?

Well, that's a good question, doctor, and I've thought about that a lot, actually. I really have. Because, you know, you try to figure out what exactly is wrong with your own brain when it starts acting up like this. And I've tried to narrow it down. Like, is it just being up high? Because I work in HR, right, and our main office building downtown, it's pretty tall. I sometimes have to go up to the 15th floor for meetings with the executives, and I can stand right there at the window, looking down at the street, watching the little cars go by, and... nothing. My palms don't sweat, my chest doesn't tighten up. I feel totally fine. I can even look down over the railing at the mall, you know, the big one with the glass elevators? No problem at all. I don't get dizzy, I don't feel like I'm going to fall. 

But then, if I'm driving, and it's a bridge... that's when it hits me. Now, to be fair, it is the big, high bridges that really get me going. The ones that arc way up over the water, where you feel like you're driving up into the sky before you level out. Those are the absolute worst. But even the smaller ones, the ones that just go over a river or a set of train tracks, if they have that certain look to them—you know, the concrete barriers, the feeling that you're suspended and there's no shoulder to pull over on—I still get that tight feeling in my chest. It's not as severe as the huge bay bridges, but it's still there. It's the structure itself, the fact that I'm on a bridge, in a car, and I'm trapped on this thing until I get to the other side. So, I guess what I'm saying is, the height definitely makes the fear worse, much worse, but the core of the problem, the thing that actually triggers the panic, is the bridge itself. It's just... bridges. If that makes any sense.
Do you experience the same level of anxiety when you're a passenger in a car crossing a bridge, or is it only when you're driving?

You know, doctor, that is... I really don't know. I honestly couldn't tell you for sure. Because, well, I'm almost always the one driving. My wife, she really doesn't care for driving in the city traffic, so whenever we go anywhere together, I'm the one behind the wheel. We just have this routine, you see. Like on the weekends, if we go to visit her sister over on the east side—which, thankfully, doesn't require crossing any major bridges, just a little overpass by the old shopping center—I'm always the one driving my sedan. 

And for work, obviously, I commute alone. I did try carpooling for a little while back in, oh, it must have been 2018 or maybe 2019? But the guy I rode with, Dave from accounting, he ended up getting transferred to another branch, and honestly, our schedules never really lined up right anyway. In HR, you end up dealing with a lot of late-afternoon employee issues and you can't just clock out at five on the dot. So, because of all that, I haven't actually been a passenger going over a big bridge in... gosh, it has to be years. 

I've tried to imagine it, though. Sometimes I sit there at my kitchen table, mapping out my alternate routes, and I think to myself, 'What if I just took a taxi or an Uber? Would that fix it?' But then my mind just starts spinning its wheels. Would it be worse because I'm totally out of control of the vehicle? You know, putting my life in the hands of some stranger who might not be paying attention? Or would it be better because I wouldn't have to worry about my own hands jerking the steering wheel over the edge? I just... I really don't know. I haven't put myself in that situation to find out. I just avoid the bridges entirely, so I haven't been in the passenger seat for one to even tell you if the panic is the same.
Do you think your anxiety would be less severe if you were a passenger in a car crossing a bridge, rather than the driver?

Well, doctor, like I was just saying... I really couldn't say for sure. I mean, it's a good question, it really is, and it's something I've tossed around in my head a lot. Because you'd think, right? You'd think if you're not the one operating the two-ton machine, maybe some of that pressure comes off. But then again, when you're the passenger, you have absolutely zero control. None. You're just sitting there, completely at the mercy of whoever is driving. What if they sneeze? What if they drop their phone and reach for it? What if a gust of wind hits the car and they overcorrect? 

I sit there sometimes and try to visualize it—being in the passenger seat, maybe my wife is driving, or an Uber driver, like I mentioned—and my chest still gets a little tight just picturing it. Because the bridge is still there. The water is still down there. The edge is still right there. But since I haven't actually done it in so long... I just don't have a concrete answer for you. I haven't tested the theory because the whole point of my routine is to avoid the bridge entirely, no matter which seat I'm sitting in. So, would it be less severe? Maybe? Or maybe it would be worse because I'd be trapped in a situation I couldn't steer myself out of. I really, honestly don't know.
Is your anxiety triggered by the thought of being on a bridge itself, or is it related to the act of driving over the bridge?

Well, doctor, bringing it back to that... I really do think it’s the bridge itself. Just the reality of being up on that structure. Because, look, I’m a rational guy, mostly. I sit at my desk in HR, I deal with facts and paperwork and employee policies all day long, so I try to look at things logically. And logically, in my head, I know those bridges over the bay are built fine. I know they have teams of engineers and city inspectors checking the steel and the concrete, and folks drive them every single day. Thousands of people, right? Commuting back and forth to the city, listening to their morning radio shows, drinking their coffee, not even giving the bridge a second thought. 

But me? When I get near one, or even just start approaching the on-ramp for one of those big spans, all that logic just completely goes right out the window. It just vanishes. My mind acts like the car could go right over the side. Just... right over the edge, past the concrete barrier, and down into the water. It’s like my brain is absolutely convinced that a gust of wind or a blown tire is going to send the whole vehicle plummeting over the railing. 

So it doesn't really matter if my hands are on the steering wheel or if I'm just picturing being in the passenger seat like we were just talking about. It’s the fact that the car is up there on that bridge in the first place, suspended over nothing, that sets off the alarm bells in my head. It’s the bridge, doctor. It's always the bridge.
Have you ever been a pedestrian on a bridge, and if so, did you experience anxiety in that situation?

Well, a pedestrian? Walking across? Oh, gosh... no, no, I haven't done that. I mean, I can't even imagine. Just thinking about walking across one of those big spans over the bay... my palms are actually getting a little sweaty right now just picturing it. 

Because, you see, if I'm in a car, at least there's this... this heavy metal box around me, right? Even if my brain is telling me the car is going to go over the edge, there's still a physical barrier between me and the outside world. But walking? Just me, in my shoes, out there in the open air with nothing but a railing between me and a hundred-foot drop into the water? No. Absolutely not. 

I remember, years ago, back when my wife and I were first dating—this was way before I got the job in HR, back when I was still working retail and trying to figure things out—we went to this state park. And they had this footbridge. Not a massive suspension bridge or anything, just a wooden footbridge over a gorge. A little tourist thing. She wanted to walk across it to take pictures of the waterfall on the other side. And I tried, doctor, I really did. I put one foot on those wooden planks, and I looked down between the cracks at the river rushing way, way down below, and my knees just locked up. Completely froze. I felt dizzy, my heart started hammering against my ribs like it was trying to escape, and I had to back away. I couldn't do it. She ended up going across by herself while I sat on a bench near the trail head, feeling like a complete fool. 

So, a pedestrian on one of those huge city bridges? With the wind whipping around and the cars rushing past you at sixty miles an hour, shaking the concrete? I haven't done it, and I wouldn't do it. I avoid driving over them, so there's absolutely no way you'd catch me trying to walk across one. I just... I don't think my heart could take it, to be perfectly honest with you.
Have you ever experienced anxiety when considering being on a bridge in any other context, such as on a bus or a train?

Well, doctor, a bus or a train... gosh, you know, I really don't know. I haven't really had to think about that, to be honest. I mean, my daily routine, the way my life is set up right now, I just drive my own car to the HR office, or my wife drives us to the grocery store or over to her sister's place. We don't really take public transit. It's just not something that comes up in my day-to-day life, you know? 

But if I really stop and think about it... if I try to picture myself on a bus going over that same bridge... well, it's hard to say. Because on the one hand, a bus is huge, right? It's heavy. It feels a lot more substantial than my little sedan. So maybe that would feel safer? But then again, you're so high up in those bus seats. You're looking right down over the railing, right down into the water. And you're completely out of control. It goes back to what I was saying earlier about being a passenger in a car. You're just sitting there, trusting this bus driver you've never met, hoping they don't make a mistake or that the wind doesn't catch that big, flat side of the bus. 

And a train? I don't even know if there are trains that go over the bridges around here, but if there were... I suppose a train is on tracks, which seems like it would be harder to fall off the edge. But it's still up there. It's still suspended over the bay. 

So, honestly, doctor, I just don't have a good answer for you on that one. I haven't been on a bus or a train over a bridge in... well, I can't even remember the last time. Maybe when I was a kid? But I wasn't afraid of bridges back then. This whole thing, this fear, it really just started creeping up on me in the last few years. So as far as buses and trains go today, I really couldn't tell you if it would trigger that same panic. I just avoid the bridges altogether, no matter how I'd be crossing them.
Would your anxiety be the same if you were to cross a very low bridge, one that is just a few feet over a small stream?

A low bridge? Like, just over a creek or a little stream somewhere? Oh, no, no, that's completely different. That doesn't bother me at all. If it's just a few feet up... say, like that little stone bridge over by the municipal golf course, where the water is barely trickling over the rocks... I drive over that without even blinking. I mean, worst case scenario there, what happens? You bump the curb, maybe you get a flat tire, or if you somehow went off the edge, you just splash into two feet of muddy water and need to call a tow truck. It's an inconvenience, sure, a huge headache for the insurance paperwork—and believe me, dealing with employee files in HR all day, I know enough about paperwork headaches—but it's not a life-or-death thing. 

But see, it really all comes back to what I was trying to explain earlier about the big ones. Because... well, I know those bridges over the bay are built fine. I really do. I know folks drive them every single day, thousands of commuters just zipping right across, drinking their coffee, totally fine. But for me, when I get near one of those massive ones, it’s just... my mind completely overrides all that common sense. It just acts like the car could go right over the side. Just straight over the edge and plummeting down into the deep water. 

With a little stream, there's no terrifying drop. But those bay bridges... you're up in the clouds, practically. And my brain just pictures the tires slipping, the steering wheel jerking, and suddenly we're breaking through that concrete barrier. It's the height, doctor, and the drop. If I'm just driving over a culvert or a little brook where I can see the bottom, my heart rate doesn't even go up a single beat. I could park on a bridge like that all day long and eat my lunch. But you put me anywhere near the approach for a bay bridge, and all that logic about how safe they are just evaporates. I just see the car tumbling over the side. Does that make sense? It's just a totally different feeling when there's a hundred-foot drop involved.
Would your anxiety be triggered by a bridge that is high above the ground but has a solid wall or barrier on both sides, so you can't see the drop?

You know, doctor, you would think a solid wall would make all the difference in the world. My wife actually asked me that exact same thing once. We were driving up north to see her cousin—this was a couple of years ago, right around the time the company was making us switch to this new payroll system at work. Which, let me tell you, was an absolute nightmare to learn. I never actually finished high school, so sitting in these HR seminars trying to understand all this complicated new software... well, it’s stressful enough without adding a tense road trip to the mix. 

But anyway, we were on this route and there was this huge elevated highway overpass, really high up, but it had these massive concrete barriers on both sides. Sound walls, I guess they were? She said to me, "Look, you can't even see over it, it's just like driving in a tunnel or a regular road."

But the thing is, my brain *knows* what's on the other side of that wall. It knows we're way up in the sky. So, even with the wall completely blocking the view of the drop, it really doesn't stop what happens to my body. Honestly, as soon as I see the bridge coming up, my chest gets tight, my hands sweat on the wheel, and I start staring straight ahead like I just have to make it to the other side. I don't look left, I don't look right at those concrete walls, I just lock my eyes on the bumper of the car in front of me or the yellow line on the asphalt and freeze up. 

It's funny how logic just completely goes right out the window in a situation like that. Because logically, a ten-foot thick concrete wall means I'm safe, right? I couldn't drive through that if I tried, not in my little sedan. But the fear doesn't care about the wall. It just cares about the height. The second I see that incline in the distance, the second I know we're going up into the air, all that anxiety just floods right back in. So, yeah, walls or no walls, if it's high up, my body just reacts the exact same way. I just grip that wheel, hold my breath, and pray for solid ground.
Would your anxiety be the same if you were to drive over a bridge that is not over water, but still very high up?

Oh, you mean like one of those massive highway overpasses? Or like a bridge over a valley or a gorge or something like that? Gosh, you know... yeah, I think it would be exactly the same. Because, like I was trying to say a minute ago about the walls, it really just boils down to the height. 

I mean, water, land, concrete, a forest... if you fall a hundred feet, it's not going to end well either way, right? My mind just plays that same horrible movie on a loop regardless of what's underneath. I remember we had to go to this regional HR conference a few years back, over in the next county. This was before they moved all our training to Zoom, which, honestly, thank goodness for Zoom, because it saves me so much driving and so much stress. But anyway, to get to this conference center, we had to take this massive flyover ramp to get onto the interstate. You know the kind I'm talking about? Where they curve way, way up in the air, looping over three or four other highways? You're just suspended up there on this thin little ribbon of concrete.

And I was sitting there, gripping the wheel, and I accidentally glanced over the side—which I know I shouldn't do, I always tell myself to just look at the license plate in front of me—but I looked, and I just saw the roofs of these huge semi-trucks passing way underneath us. They looked like little toy cars down there. And my stomach just dropped right out of me. It wasn't water, it was just asphalt and traffic down below, but the panic was identical. The sweaty palms, the tight chest, the feeling like I couldn't get a full breath... it's the dropping, doctor. The falling. 

If I'm up in the air, my brain just tells me I'm going to fall. It doesn't matter if I'm falling into a bay or onto a parking lot. It's that feeling of being disconnected from the earth, just hanging up there where cars aren't supposed to be. So, yeah, water or no water, if it's high up, I'm going to be an absolute nervous wreck until my tires are back on solid, flat ground. I just can't shake that feeling of gravity just waiting to pull the car down.
Would your anxiety be triggered if someone else was driving you over the bridge, but you were not driving?

You know, that's a really interesting question, doctor, and I... well, I honestly don't know for sure. Because, see, I almost never let anyone else drive me. I really don't. Especially not if I know we're going somewhere that might involve crossing a bridge or even just taking the interstate. 

My wife, she offers all the time. She’s got this nice little crossover SUV, very smooth ride, and she always says, "Just let me drive for once, you can lean the seat back, close your eyes, and listen to the radio." And it sounds nice in theory, it really does. But I just... I can't bring myself to give up that control, you know? I think about sitting in that passenger seat, and part of me wonders if maybe it would be a little better because I wouldn't have to be the one steering, but then my brain immediately goes, well, what if it's worse? What if she drives too close to the edge? What if a big truck blows past and she overcorrects? 

Even at work, when we have to do those HR team-building retreats—which, don't even get me started on those, trying to organize carpools for a dozen people who all want to leave at different times is just a massive headache—but whenever we do them, I always volunteer to drive my own car. Always. I tell the folks at the office that I just prefer driving, but the truth is, I need to be behind the wheel so I can control the route. If I'm driving, I can take the back roads, I can avoid the big overpasses, I can make sure we stay on solid ground. If I'm in the backseat of Gary from Accounting's minivan, I'm totally at his mercy. And if he decides to take the scenic route over a suspension bridge, I'm trapped. 

So, to be completely honest with you, I haven't really been in a situation where someone else actually drove me over one of those massive drops in... gosh, it has to be years and years. I just avoid letting it happen at all costs. So I really couldn't tell you if the panic would be triggered the exact same way, or if it would be less, or maybe even double. I just know the thought of being a passenger makes me squirm, but I haven't actually put it to the test to see how my body would react.
Is your anxiety triggered by the height of the bridge, or is it the fact that it's a bridge, regardless of its height?

Well, it's... it's definitely the height, doctor. I mean, if it's just a little wooden bridge over a creek in the park, or one of those tiny little stone things you drive over in a residential neighborhood where it's maybe three feet off the ground, I don't bat an eye. I don't even really register it as a bridge, to be honest. It's just part of the road. So it's not the actual concept of a bridge that gets me worked up. It's the drop. It's always the drop. 

Like, you take those massive bridges over the bay, right? The ones that stretch for miles and go way, way up in the air to let the big cargo ships pass underneath. Now, logically, I know those bridges over the bay are built perfectly fine. I mean, structural engineers spent years designing them, they use thousands of tons of steel, and folks drive them every single day without a second thought. We've got plenty of people in our office, folks I process payroll for every two weeks, who commute from across the bay. They just swipe their badges in the morning and complain about the traffic on the bridge, but never the bridge itself. They're probably listening to the radio or drinking their morning coffee, completely relaxed while they're suspended hundreds of feet in the air. 

But me? When I even get near one, when I just see that huge structure looming up ahead on the highway, my mind just completely short-circuits. It just acts like the car could go right over the side at any second. I picture the tires slipping, or a gust of wind catching the side of my sedan, or some other driver bumping my quarter panel, and suddenly we're just plunging over the guardrail and down into the water. It doesn't matter how thick the concrete is or how safe I know it is in my rational brain. The height just triggers this absolute, terrifying certainty that my car is going to go over the edge. 

So, yeah, if a bridge is basically flat on the ground, I'm right as rain. I could drive over it a hundred times. But you put me up in the clouds, and all rationality just disappears entirely. It's the height that plays tricks on my mind.
Is it the height of the bridge itself that triggers your anxiety, or is it something about being on a bridge in general?

Well, like I think I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, it's really just the height. The bridge itself isn't the problem at all. 

I mean, I can elaborate on that a bit more if it helps, because it is kind of an interesting distinction when you really get down to it. There's actually this little overpass right near the HR office—just a small concrete slab over a drainage ditch, maybe two or three feet off the dirt. I drive over it every single day, usually twice a day depending on if I run out to grab lunch, and I never even think about it. My tires hit it, it makes a little *thump-thump* sound, and that's it. No sweaty palms, no gripping the steering wheel, nothing. I don't even register it as a bridge, honestly, it's just another piece of the road to me. 

But it's funny you ask again, because it really gets me thinking about exactly *why* my brain reacts the way it does. I guess it really just comes down to that feeling of gravity. If a bridge is flat on the ground, gravity isn't going to do anything to me if something goes wrong. If the car breaks down or someone bumps my fender, I just pull over onto the grass. But if I'm up high, it's like my brain is suddenly doing all this terrible math, calculating the drop, picturing the fall, wondering if the guardrails are strong enough to hold a two-ton car. 

So, yeah, just to reiterate what I was saying before, it's 100 percent the height. A bridge is really just a road until somebody decides to build it way up in the clouds. Once it's up there, that's when it turns into this whole other terrifying thing for me. But the bridge part? No, that part is totally fine.
Is your anxiety triggered by the act of crossing the bridge, or is it solely due to the height of the bridge?

Well, I guess... I mean, the height is the root of the whole problem, right? Like I was saying. But the actual act of crossing it, being the one in the car having to get from point A to point B over that drop, that's when all the physical stuff really kicks in. 

It's like, I can know a tall bridge is on my route, say if I'm looking at a map or trying to plan out a drive for a weekend trip. I'll hate the idea of it, and I'll try to find a detour, but I'm not sitting there panicking at my kitchen table. But being in the car, actually having to do the crossing? That's a whole different animal. 

As soon as I see the bridge coming up—you know, when it just starts looming over the highway and you pass that last exit sign and realize you are totally locked in and there's no turning back—that's when it hits me. My chest gets tight, just incredibly tight, like somebody cinched a belt right around my ribs and won't let go. And my hands sweat on the wheel. I mean, they get absolutely clammy. I've got this steering wheel cover on my car, just a cheap faux-leather one I picked up at the auto parts store a few years back because the original grip was peeling off, and my palms get so slick against it that I have to squeeze extra hard just to feel like I'm in control of the vehicle. 

And then, once my tires actually hit that incline and I'm on the bridge, I just sort of freeze up. I start staring straight ahead, just dead ahead, like I just have to make it to the other side. I won't look left at the water, I won't look right, I don't even like checking my rearview mirror. I just lock my eyes on the white dashes on the road or the license plate of the car in front of me, and I get this intense tunnel vision. It's like my whole body goes into survival mode just to get through the actual crossing of it. So I guess you could say the height is the reason I'm terrified, but the act of actually driving over it is what makes my body go completely haywire like that.
Is your anxiety triggered by the height of the bridge or by something else about the bridge itself?

I know I keep repeating myself here, doc, but I really don't know how else to explain it—it's just the height. There's absolutely nothing else about the bridge itself that bothers me. It's not the asphalt, it's not the suspension cables, it's not the toll booths or the painted lines. It's purely the fact that it's way up in the air. 

Like I was mentioning before with those big bridges over the bay. I mean, I sit there at my desk in the HR department, processing direct deposit forms and managing benefits for all these people who commute across the water every single morning. I see them come into the office, grab their coffee, totally fine. So I know those bridges over the bay are built fine. I know they're structurally sound and folks drive them every single day without a second thought. But for me... well, when I get near one, all that rational thinking just completely flies right out the window. My mind just acts like the car could go right over the side at any given second. 

If you took that exact same bridge, with the exact same concrete and the exact same guardrails, and you laid it flat on the dirt, I wouldn't care one bit. I'd drive right over it. But because it's elevated, because there's that massive drop underneath it, my brain just convinces me that my tires are going to slip and I'm going to plunge over the edge. So it really isn't the bridge itself. It's just the height.

target_item.reason: The doctor is trying to clarify the exact nature of the specific phobic fear (whether it is the height or the bridge itself), which maps to the Specific Phobic Fear symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... it's definitely the height, doctor. I mean, if it's just a little wooden bridge over a creek in the park, or one of those tiny little stone things you drive over in a residential neighborhood where it's maybe three feet off the ground, I don't bat an eye. I don't even really register it as a bridge, to be honest. It's just part of the road. So it's not the actual concept of a bridge that gets me worked up. It's the drop. It's always the drop. 

Like, you take those massive bridges over the bay, right? The ones that stretch for miles and go way, way up in the air to let the big cargo ships pass underneath. Now, logically, I know those bridges over the bay are built perfectly fine. I mean, structural engineers spent years designing them, they use thousands of tons of steel, and folks drive them every single day without a second thought. We've got plenty of people in our office, folks I process payroll for every two weeks, who commute from across the bay. They just swipe their badges in the morning and complain about the traffic on the bridge, but never the bridge itself. They're probably listening to the radio or drinking their morning coffee, completely relaxed while they're suspended hundreds of feet in the air. 

But me? When I even get near one, when I just see that huge structure looming up ahead on the highway, my mind just completely short-circuits. It just acts like the car could go right over the side at any second. I picture the tires slipping, or a gust of wind catching the side of my sedan, or some other driver bumping my quarter panel, and suddenly we're just plunging over the guardrail and down into the water. It doesn't matter how thick the concrete is or how safe I know it is in my rational brain. The height just triggers this absolute, terrifying certainty that my car is going to go over the edge. 

So, yeah, if a bridge is basically flat on the ground, I'm right as rain. I could drive over it a hundred times. But you put me up in the clouds, and all rationality just disappears entirely. It's the height that plays tricks on my mind.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is triggered by the height of the bridge or the fact that it's a bridge
doctor.question: Is it the height of the bridge itself that triggers your anxiety, or is it something about being on a bridge in general?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeating the exact same question about whether the trigger is the height or the bridge in general, which the patient just answered in the previous turn using the Specific_Phobic_Fear item. There are no other items in the symptom profile that address this question.

patient.answer:
Well, like I think I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, it's really just the height. The bridge itself isn't the problem at all. 

I mean, I can elaborate on that a bit more if it helps, because it is kind of an interesting distinction when you really get down to it. There's actually this little overpass right near the HR office—just a small concrete slab over a drainage ditch, maybe two or three feet off the dirt. I drive over it every single day, usually twice a day depending on if I run out to grab lunch, and I never even think about it. My tires hit it, it makes a little *thump-thump* sound, and that's it. No sweaty palms, no gripping the steering wheel, nothing. I don't even register it as a bridge, honestly, it's just another piece of the road to me. 

But it's funny you ask again, because it really gets me thinking about exactly *why* my brain reacts the way it does. I guess it really just comes down to that feeling of gravity. If a bridge is flat on the ground, gravity isn't going to do anything to me if something goes wrong. If the car breaks down or someone bumps my fender, I just pull over onto the grass. But if I'm up high, it's like my brain is suddenly doing all this terrible math, calculating the drop, picturing the fall, wondering if the guardrails are strong enough to hold a two-ton car. 

So, yeah, just to reiterate what I was saying before, it's 100 percent the height. A bridge is really just a road until somebody decides to build it way up in the clouds. Once it's up there, that's when it turns into this whole other terrifying thing for me. But the bridge part? No, that part is totally fine.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is triggered by the height of the bridge or the act of crossing it
doctor.question: Is your anxiety triggered by the act of crossing the bridge, or is it solely due to the height of the bridge?

target_item.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
target_item.manifestation: As soon as I see the bridge coming up, my chest gets tight, my hands sweat on the wheel, and I start staring straight ahead like I just have to make it to the other side.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about what triggers the anxiety (the act of crossing vs. the height). The manifestation for S063 describes the immediate physical anxiety response triggered as soon as the patient sees the bridge coming up to cross it.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess... I mean, the height is the root of the whole problem, right? Like I was saying. But the actual act of crossing it, being the one in the car having to get from point A to point B over that drop, that's when all the physical stuff really kicks in. 

It's like, I can know a tall bridge is on my route, say if I'm looking at a map or trying to plan out a drive for a weekend trip. I'll hate the idea of it, and I'll try to find a detour, but I'm not sitting there panicking at my kitchen table. But being in the car, actually having to do the crossing? That's a whole different animal. 

As soon as I see the bridge coming up—you know, when it just starts looming over the highway and you pass that last exit sign and realize you are totally locked in and there's no turning back—that's when it hits me. My chest gets tight, just incredibly tight, like somebody cinched a belt right around my ribs and won't let go. And my hands sweat on the wheel. I mean, they get absolutely clammy. I've got this steering wheel cover on my car, just a cheap faux-leather one I picked up at the auto parts store a few years back because the original grip was peeling off, and my palms get so slick against it that I have to squeeze extra hard just to feel like I'm in control of the vehicle. 

And then, once my tires actually hit that incline and I'm on the bridge, I just sort of freeze up. I start staring straight ahead, just dead ahead, like I just have to make it to the other side. I won't look left at the water, I won't look right, I don't even like checking my rearview mirror. I just lock my eyes on the white dashes on the road or the license plate of the car in front of me, and I get this intense tunnel vision. It's like my whole body goes into survival mode just to get through the actual crossing of it. So I guess you could say the height is the reason I'm terrified, but the act of actually driving over it is what makes my body go completely haywire like that.

target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about the specific trigger of the anxiety (height vs. the bridge itself), which relates to the specific phobic fear.

patient.answer:
I know I keep repeating myself here, doc, but I really don't know how else to explain it—it's just the height. There's absolutely nothing else about the bridge itself that bothers me. It's not the asphalt, it's not the suspension cables, it's not the toll booths or the painted lines. It's purely the fact that it's way up in the air. 

Like I was mentioning before with those big bridges over the bay. I mean, I sit there at my desk in the HR department, processing direct deposit forms and managing benefits for all these people who commute across the water every single morning. I see them come into the office, grab their coffee, totally fine. So I know those bridges over the bay are built fine. I know they're structurally sound and folks drive them every single day without a second thought. But for me... well, when I get near one, all that rational thinking just completely flies right out the window. My mind just acts like the car could go right over the side at any given second. 

If you took that exact same bridge, with the exact same concrete and the exact same guardrails, and you laid it flat on the dirt, I wouldn't care one bit. I'd drive right over it. But because it's elevated, because there's that massive drop underneath it, my brain just convinces me that my tires are going to slip and I'm going to plunge over the edge. So it really isn't the bridge itself. It's just the height.
